title: A contact path for a recruiting firm
metaTitle: A contact path for a recruiting firm
excerpt: Say what happens after a hiring manager writes, how soon you reply, and what they should have ready. A ten-field form is how you lose the brief.
alt: A person in a blue shirt signing a paper document with a pen, a formal signature standing in for a brief that should be shorter than a contract.
caption: The brief should not feel like a document they have to sign blind. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a recruiting contact page say before the form?
faqs.answer: Say what happens next: you read the brief, you reply with whether you take this kind of search, and you name the kind of person who answers. Say what the reply is not, including a shortlist. Put that promise above the fields, in lines a phone can show without scrolling.

faqs.question: How many fields should the brief form have?
faqs.answer: Stay at about five: role title, company or company shape, why the seat is open, what the last attempt got wrong, and a way to reply. Cut industry dropdowns, budget ranges, and required uploads. Ask for the org chart after you have agreed to run the search.

faqs.question: Should the page promise a reply time?
faqs.answer: Only if the team can keep it on a bad week. A window such as two set days is better than the word promptly. If the window slips, change the page. Do not publish an hour you cannot honor because it looks attentive.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A recruiting firm contact page should tell a hiring manager who has been burned before what happens after they reach out, how soon they will hear back, and what to have ready. The action is to brief the search. A form with ten fields is a way to lose them. Nielsen Norman Group's research is the reason to keep it short: people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and the first 10 seconds decide whether they stay. A form that looks like a procurement portal spends that time on your process, not on their role.

Write the page as a promise you can keep. If you cannot say who replies, do not imply a named partner will. If you cannot say when, do not invent a clock for the layout. A missing number is better than a number the office does not honor.

## What happens after they send

Say the next three beats in order, above the form.

You read the brief. You reply with whether this is a search you take. If it is, you say what the first conversation covers and who will be on it. If it is not, you say so. A burned buyer is listening for the handoff to a coordinator who cannot answer. Name the kind of person who replies: the person who would run the search, or a researcher who can decline. Do not write "a member of our team."

Say what the reply is not. It is not a shortlist. It is not a proposal with candidate names. It is a yes, a no, or a request for one missing fact. That boundary keeps you from overpromising in the label of the button.

Put this in three short lines, not a paragraph of welcome. The lines should be visible without scrolling on a phone. The form comes after the promise. A form that arrives first trains the buyer to fill boxes before they know why.

If you book the first conversation from this page, the event title should be the brief, and the confirmation should repeat the three beats. A calendar link that says "30 minute intro" with no mention of the role is a different product. Use it only if that is truly what they get.

## How fast, said as a promise you keep

Speed is part of trust only when it is true. If a partner reads briefs twice a week, say that. "We reply on Tuesday and Friday" is a clock a buyer can test. "We respond promptly" is a word they have already heard from the firm that went quiet.

Do not publish "within one hour" because it looks attentive. Publish the window the person who actually replies can keep on a bad week. If the window slips, change the page the same day. An outdated promise is a small lie, and this buyer collects small lies.

If the search is confidential and you need to check conflicts before you reply, say that the first note may only confirm you received it and that a real answer follows after the conflict check. Give the outer bound. A silence with no bound feels like the last search.

The same honesty applies to holidays and to a partner's travel. You do not need a live status board. You need one sentence the team agrees to. Read it in the Monday meeting until it is boring. Boring means it is true.

## What they should have ready

Ask for the minimum that lets you say yes or no.

The role title. The company, by name or by shape if they are not ready to name it. Why the seat is open. What the last attempt got wrong. A way to reply.

That is enough to know whether you fill this kind of role. You do not need compensation philosophy, an org chart, a diversity statement, or the names of every stakeholder before the first reply. Those belong in the search, after you have agreed to run it. Asking for them on the contact page is how you look like the firm that billed for intake.

W3C's WCAG 2 overview puts forms under a standard organized into perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. The understandable principle is the one this page lives or dies on. Each field needs a label that says what it is, in the buyer's words. "Role title" is a label. "Requirement" is not. If they make an error, the message should say how to fix it, next to the field, not as a red banner at the top that does not name the problem.

Do not use placeholder text as the only label. It disappears when they type, and it often fails contrast. A visible label can stay. The field can be large enough to tap. A row of tiny inputs is a desktop habit. On a phone it is a reason to leave.

## Why ten fields lose this buyer

Count the fields. If you are over five, cut. The usual excess is: company size, industry dropdown with forty options, budget range, how they heard of you, a required phone number, an upload for a job description, a checkbox for a privacy novel, and a second checkbox for a newsletter.

Industry dropdowns are where a burned buyer feels the wideness of the last search. Forty industries say you fill everything. A free line for company shape is more honest. Budget ranges before they have seen your fee shape turn the brief into a haggle. How-they-heard-of-you is an internal report. It can be optional and last, or absent.

A required upload stops people who are writing from a phone. Let them paste three lines. You can ask for a document after you accept the search.

One checkbox for a real privacy note is enough, written in a sentence, linking to the note. A newsletter box pre-checked is a dark pattern this buyer will notice. Leave it off, or do not ask.

## The confirmation is part of the page

The thank-you state should repeat what happens next, in the same words as the promise above the form. "We have the role. You will hear whether we take this kind of search." If you said Tuesday and Friday, repeat that. Do not swap in "soon."

Send the same words by email, from a named address a buyer can reply to. A no-reply address tells them the relationship is already a ticket. If the email and the page disagree, fix the email. The page is the contract they can see. The email is the contract that arrives when they are no longer looking at it.

If you decline, decline in a sentence that restates the kind of role you do fill. A silent archive is how a maybe becomes a grudge. You do not owe a long explanation. You owe a clear no.

Keep a copy of what they sent somewhere the person who replies will actually see it. A form that lands in a shared inbox nobody owns is not a contact path. It is a drawer. Assign the drawer before you publish the form.

## Read the last ten briefs against the form

Pull the last ten messages that started a search, including the ones you declined. Mark every fact you actually used to decide. If a fact was not on the form, either add that one field or admit you asked for it on the call. If a field on the form never changed a decision, remove it. The form should be a record of how you choose work, not a copy of a CRM someone's vendor recommended.

Then reply to one of those old briefs using only the new promise. If you cannot say yes or no from those fields, the form is still too thin, or your real criteria are still private. Write the missing criterion into the promise or into one field. Do not keep it in a partner's head. A criterion that lives only in a head becomes a surprise for the buyer and a quarrel inside the firm.

Do this again when you change the kind of role you fill. A form from a generalist year will keep attracting generalist briefs. The contact page is how the homepage's sentence gets tested by strangers. If the two disagree, fix the form the same week you fix the sentence.

## Other doors, without splitting the path

A phone number and an email can sit under the form for people who will not use it. They should reach the same promise. If email is the real path, do not also offer a phone number that goes to a receptionist who cannot take a brief. One path, with a spare door that lands in the same place.

Do not add a chat widget that opens with "How can we help?" The widget throws away the structure you just wrote. If you truly answer chat with the same three beats, say so in the first automated line, and make the handoff to a human match the page. Most firms cannot. Take the widget off.

The page is finished when a skeptic can say what they will get, by when, and what they must prepare, without asking you. Then remove everything else. The next edit is usually subtraction. Read [what to take off the rest of the site](/blog/what-not-to-put-on-the-site-for-a-recruiting-firm) before you add a sidebar of values next to this form.

If you want help shaping the path from a first screen to a brief a team will actually answer, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The form is the last step, not the first design.
